title: A Confirmatory Paired Evaluation of Generate→Verify→Repair vs LLM‑Only NetOps Suggestions: A Null Result on a Deterministic Synthetic Task Pool
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop) comparing a generate→verify→repair (G→V→R) pipeline to an LLM‑only suggestion pipeline for intent→configuration NetOps tasks. Using a deterministic task generator and a deterministic validator, we sampled K=200 paired tasks and ran a single shared initial generation per task with the requested_model gpt-5-mini. The preregistered primary estimand was the paired difference in regression‑causing change rate (guarded − baseline). Observed outcome: baseline = 200/200 successful validator‑compliant applies, guarded = 200/200; paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) 95% percentile CI = [0.00,0.00]. The repair loop was never invoked (repair_applied = 0 across pairs). We release the complete preregistration, model/provider traces, validator traces, deterministic reconciliation, and analysis artifacts (see execution/* and analysis/* in the evidence bundle) so others can replay and extend the design. We interpret the null as a ceiling effect under the chosen task/model/validator conditions and discuss implications for future confirmatory designs seeking to demonstrate verifier/repair value.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation is a high‑value NetOps objective, but erroneous proposals can cause regressions with operational impact. Architectures that pair a stochastic generator (an LLM) with a deterministic verifier and a constrained repair step—i.e., generate→verify→repair (G→V→R)—are advocated to reduce regressions by checking and correcting candidate changes before apply. Prior empirical work and benchmarks argue for verifier integration, but comparative claims are sensitive to task selection, generator error rates, and verifier coverage. To obtain a defensible, reproducible estimate of the marginal value of a verifier+repair layer, we preregistered a paired confirmatory experiment that holds generation fixed across arms and measures whether deterministic verification and a single automatic repair invocation reduce regression‑causing changes relative to accepting the generator output directly.
We selected a narrow but operationally meaningful task family (intent_configuration_repair_v1) and froze the complete experimental plan in a machine‑readable preregistration (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop; preregistration SHA‑256 a6d73a5cc0bda22e691a3634068a881b36ae274a65ab33919a647ec32c56e622). The run used the requested_model gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa) and deterministic components: deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Our confirmatory design and full artifact recording (responses, provider calls, validator traces, and hash manifests) enable exact replay and independent auditing of every principal number reported below.
sections.related_work: Recent literature outlines two complementary streams relevant to this study. First, LLM‑driven NetOps research demonstrates that large models can synthesize router/switch configuration fragments from high‑level intents, sometimes matching human drafts on straightforward tasks. Second, verification and formal‑model approaches (e.g., Batfish/NetKAT style verifiers and recent generate‑validate‑repair benchmarks) aim to bound risk by checking semantic effects (reachability, must‑stay invariants, canary constraints) before applying changes. Position pieces emphasize that operational reliability depends on the machinery surrounding LLMs (tooling, validators, rollback), not on generator fluency alone. Our study isolates the marginal effect of inserting a deterministic verifier+repair layer when generator outputs are identical across arms; this complements prior work that varies generators or integrates generator–verifier interaction loops. We reference the nearest methodological antecedents (Cornetto and related generate‑validate‑repair pipelines) as motivation and used their conceptual framing when designing the verifier semantics and the scoring rule full_intent_constraint_validation (see cited_record_ids).
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The preregistration froze the study question, the primary hypothesis H1, sampling rules, validator and generator identifiers, maximum model call budget, and the exact analysis procedure. The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline: the absolute difference in regression‑causing change rate between the guarded (G→V→R) and baseline (LLM‑only) arms, paired within task. Power planning assumed baseline failure ≈0.20 and targeted an absolute reduction of 0.08 with two‑sided alpha=0.05 and power=0.80; sensitivity scans were preregistered.
Task sampling and pair construction. Tasks were deterministically assembled from a public synthetic pool produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Inclusion required preregistered validator coverage. The deterministic sampling rule was: compute SHA‑256(intent_string), sort ascending, and select the first K=200 tasks (documented in execution/task_manifest.jsonl, SHA‑256 f1d447b7...). This removes subjective selection and enables byte‑exact replay. Each sampled intent produced one shared initial generator output (shared_initial_generation) that was evaluated in both arms (baseline and guarded). This paired/shared generation design isolates verifier/repair marginal effect by holding the generator output constant across arms.
Generator, validator, and repair policy. The requested generator was gpt-5-mini; provider and request logs are in execution/provider_calls/*.json. The validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5, version 5.0) executes a structured parse of the candidate configuration, applies workflow constraints (e.g., shut‑down before MTU change, group minimum‑up constraints, protected interfaces), and yields a binary valid flag plus rich diagnostics (parsed_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, normalized_configuration, final_state snapshot). The primary scoring rule was full_intent_constraint_validation: an apply is a success if validator.valid==true. The guarded arm allowed a single repair attempt per task (maximum_repair_calls_per_task=1) using a constrained repair prompt; repaired candidate is revalidated once. All per‑episode validator traces (execution/scoring/*.json) record repair_applied and validator decision metadata.
Execution contract, logging, and provenance. The run adhered to the preregistered adapter_family hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and execution_mode scientific_confirmatory. We recorded all raw responses (execution/responses/*.txt), provider call traces (execution/provider_calls/*.json), scoring traces (execution/scoring/*.json), and an execution manifest with SHA‑256 hashes (execution/execution_manifest.json; raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 3dfbe1b6580c9df4233332164d0453e2aecdb34d52a01883358d67ac30e028e6). We logged cache hits/misses and call metadata for contamination detection; no cache reuse across conditions was observed. The master prompt provenance is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba) as required by the track.
sections.results:
Execution and primary outcome. The run completed per preregistration: planned episodes = 400 (two arms × K=200 tasks); completed episodes = 400; failed = 0; model_calls_used = 200 (one shared-generation per task). The confirmatory analysis used complete_pair_count = 200. Observed binary outcomes (success = validator.valid) were: baseline_success_count = 200/200 and guarded_success_count = 200/200. The paired contingency table is n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 7bc1bd2a...).
Statistical inference and CI. Per the analysis plan we executed an exact McNemar two‑sided test for paired binary outcomes: p = 1.00. We computed a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI with 10,000 resamples and seed=1729 (bootstrap metadata in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl); the resulting CI is [0.00,0.00]. The primary estimand point estimate (guarded − baseline) = 0.00. Because the guarded validator never flagged the shared candidate as invalid, the repair pathway was not invoked for any task (repair_applied = false in every execution/scoring/*.json trace), and no repair artifacts exist beyond recorded null flags.
Representative diagnostics. Representative episode artifacts are archived and hashed: e.g., execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt (SHA‑256 f8de4d6e...), execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json (SHA‑256 3055f874...), and execution/provider_calls/task-000001-shared-initial.json (SHA‑256 b32ec9f7...). Example validator traces include parsed_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, and final_state snapshots enabling replay of the validation semantics (see execution/scoring/*.json entries and the compact diagnostic Figure 2 caption). Provider call audit shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and cache_miss_count = 200 (no cross‑condition cache reuse detected). All deterministic reconciliation checks passed (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json SHA‑256 9b79e943...).
sections.discussion:
Null result interpretation and ceiling effect. The observed null (both arms perfect success) is a valid experimental outcome under the preregistered contract. It primarily reflects a ceiling effect: for the sampled task pool and the generator selected (gpt-5-mini), the shared generator proposals satisfied the validator's constraints in every case. Consequently the verifier+repair machinery had no opportunity to change the apply outcome; repair_applied==0 across all tasks. This demonstrates that a G→V→R pipeline can be inert when generator accuracy and validator coverage align, and that demonstrating verifier marginal value requires task/model/validator regimes with nontrivial baseline error rates.
Design implications for future confirmatory work. To detect verifier utility, confirmatory designs should ensure baseline generator error is nonzero or that task sampling includes edge cases that invite verifier blockage. Practical alternatives include: (i) sampling intents near validator coverage boundaries or adversarial intents, (ii) using weaker or a set of generator models to inflate baseline errors, (iii) adversarially perturbing generator outputs to force validator engagement, or (iv) changing the estimand to capture generator–verifier interaction (e.g., repeated generator repair cycles), which more closely mirrors agentic workflows but changes the causal estimand. Each alternative trades off internal control and interpretability for operational realism.
Limitations and threats to validity. Internal validity is strong because the experiment was deterministic and preregistered; every artifact is recorded and hashed. Construct validity is limited by the fact that validator.valid is an operational proxy for regression; the real‑world correspondence depends on validator fidelity to production execution semantics. External validity is constrained: a single requested_model (gpt-5-mini), a synthetic deterministic task pool, and the specific validator limit generalization. Conclusion validity: our preregistered power assumptions (baseline ≈0.20) did not hold; with observed baseline=1.0 the original power calculations are moot. We therefore report exact tests, bootstrap intervals, and exhaustive artifact traces to prevent overinterpretation. Reproducibility artifacts and the full manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json and hashes) are provided to enable independent replay and extension.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, artifact‑grounded paired comparison of a G→V→R pipeline versus LLM‑only suggestions for K=200 deterministic NetOps tasks. Under the chosen generator and validator, both arms produced validator‑compliant proposals on all tasks (200/200), producing a paired difference of 0.00 (McNemar p=1.00; bootstrap 95% CI=[0.00,0.00]). The repair step was not exercised. This null result documents a ceiling case: when generator proposals already satisfy deterministic validator constraints, adding a verifier+repair layer does not change the binary apply outcome. We release the complete preregistration, execution, scoring, and analysis artifacts (see execution/* and analysis/*) so future studies can replay this exact run, alter the task or generator regime, and quantify verifier/repair marginal value in settings that are failure‑rich or where generator–verifier interaction is permitted. Such designs will be essential to empirically justify the operational cost of always‑on verification for agentic NetOps workflows.

limitations: Single‑model evaluation (gpt-5-mini) — results do not generalize to other LLMs without additional experiments.
Synthetic deterministic task pool and deterministic sampling — external validity to production change intents and natural operator distributions is limited.
Primary outcome depends on deterministic_netops_validator_v5 fidelity to operational regressions; construct validity is tied to validator realism and coverage.
Ceiling effect: baseline success = 100% eliminated ability to demonstrate verifier/repair benefit under this design and sample.
Residual contamination (undetectable pretraining overlap) cannot be fully excluded despite hashing and logging; contamination_summary.csv recorded no flagged items for this run.
